transcript.content: Hi, welcome in — I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Yeah, um… I guess what brings me in is I feel like I’m always on, like I’m running on a motor. I’ll finish one thing at school, or even just something around the house, and before I’ve even really stopped I’m already onto the next thing.

I teach special education, so there’s always something happening anyway, but this feels like more than just being busy. It’s like I can’t shut myself off. Even when I’m done, I’m not really done, if that makes sense.
Has this feeling of being constantly 'on' and unable to stop been something new that started recently, or is it something you've noticed most of your life?

No, it’s definitely not new. I mean, my mother used to laugh about it—well, half laugh, half be exhausted by it, I think. She’d say even back in elementary school I was basically trying to teach the class from my seat, because I was always popping up, talking, or jumping in before the teacher even finished giving directions.

And, you know, I became a teacher myself, which is kind of funny in hindsight. But yeah, this has been part of me for as long as I can remember. It didn’t just start recently or because of any family stuff.
Have you noticed a pattern of intense, unstable relationships or a shifting sense of who you are, such as your self-image or goals changing dramatically depending on who you're with?

Um… I don’t think so? At least not in the way you’re describing, I don’t think.

I mean, relationships can be stressful like anybody’s, and I’ve had friendships where I’ll get really involved in something they’re into—like years ago a coworker got me into woodworking for about five minutes, bought the tools and everything, and then I realized I had nowhere to put the wood, which my wife was not thrilled about—but that’s probably not what you mean.

I don’t feel like I become a totally different person depending on who I’m with. And my goals haven’t really swung all over the place like that. I’ve been in teaching for a long time, same general direction. So… no, I haven’t really noticed that kind of intense unstable relationship thing or my identity shifting dramatically.

Would you say this constant 'on' feeling and difficulty stopping actually causes problems for you—like mistakes at work, trouble finishing tasks, or friction at home—or is it more just a personality trait that doesn't really interfere with your life?

No, it’s… it’s definitely causing problems. I wish it was just, you know, “that’s how I am,” because then maybe people would just roll their eyes and move on.

At work it’s gotten serious enough that I was put on a corrective plan, which was honestly embarrassing. I mean, in special ed there are already a million moving parts — forms, meetings, parents, aides needing something, the copier always jamming right when you need it, you know — but the complaints weren’t just casual. They were serious.

And at home, my spouse has said the caregiving routines are harder because people have to manage my energy on top of everything else. Like instead of me making things easier, I’m adding another layer people have to deal with. That feels awful.

I really am trying to help. That’s the part that gets me. I’m not trying to be disruptive or difficult, but I feel like I’m damaging trust with colleagues and with my family.

Have you ever had distinct periods—lasting several days or more—where you felt unusually elevated, euphoric, or irritable, needed much less sleep than usual but still felt full of energy, and this was different from your usual baseline?

I’m not sure I’d describe it that way, no. I mean, I’m “full of energy” a lot, but that’s kind of my normal, not like a separate stretch where suddenly I’m euphoric or barely sleeping and somehow better than usual.

I do get irritable when I’m overwhelmed or when there’s too much going on—like at school when three people need me at once and the schedule changes, which happens constantly—but I don’t think I’ve had several days where I’m a totally different version of myself or running on no sleep and feeling great.

So… I don’t think so. Not that I’ve noticed, anyway.
Do you often find it hard to stay focused on tasks, get easily distracted, or forget things like appointments or where you put items, even when you're trying to pay attention?

I’m not sure how to answer that cleanly. I mean, everybody loses their keys sometimes, right? My wife has this little bowl by the door that’s supposed to solve that, except then the mail ends up in the bowl, and then it’s not really a key bowl anymore, it’s just… a pile.

But, sorry, your actual question—focus and forgetting. I don’t know that I’ve tracked it enough to say “often” in a definite way. I have moments where I feel scattered, but I’m not sure if that’s more than normal or just because there’s a lot going on. I’d probably need you to narrow down what you mean, like at work versus home or appointments versus objects.

When you're doing something like filling out paperwork, reading a report, or sitting through a meeting at school, do you notice your mind wandering or losing track of what's being said, even when you're trying hard to pay attention?

I… maybe? I’m not trying to be difficult, I just don’t always notice it in the moment. Meetings at school can be a lot because someone’s talking about one student, then someone mentions transportation, then I’m thinking, “Oh, did I send that email?” and then—well, that’s sort of what you’re asking, isn’t it?

But I can’t say for sure if it’s my mind wandering in a way that’s unusual, or if the meetings themselves are just chaotic. Paperwork is its own thing too, because half the time the form asks the same question in three different ways, and I start wondering who designed it and whether they’ve ever actually worked in a classroom.

So… yes, I can lose the thread sometimes, but I don’t know how much of that is me versus the situation.
Do you often find yourself interrupting others, blurting out answers or comments before someone has finished speaking, or having trouble waiting your turn in conversations or situations?

Yeah… that one, yes. I do that more than I probably want to admit.

I’ll jump into conversations at school—like if two colleagues are talking through a student issue, or a parent is trying to explain something—and I think I’m helping because I can see where it’s going, or I think I have the solution, so I start talking before they’re really done. And then suddenly I’ve kind of taken over the conversation.

It happens at home too. My wife will be talking with a relative, and I’ll jump in to “clarify” or fix something, and then later she’ll tell me, “You didn’t let me finish,” which… yeah, she’s probably right. I don’t usually mean to be rude. It feels like I’m trying to help, but I end up talking over people.
Thinking back to before you turned 12 years old, do you remember having trouble sitting still, blurting things out, or losing focus in school, similar to what you experience now?

Yeah, that goes way back. My mother used to joke that I “taught the class from my seat,” because even in elementary school I was always out of my chair, talking, cutting in before the teacher even finished giving directions.

I mean, she said it like it was funny—families do that, they turn things into stories—but looking back, it really was kind of who I was. Not something that just appeared recently or because of, you know, changes at home or family stress. It was there when I was a kid.
